title: Two sentences
hookLine: I testify there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His messenger

lines: I TESTIFY: NO GOD BUT ALLAH.
cards: Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. If you've ever stood near a mosque at prayer time, you may have heard those words carried over the rooftops in the call to prayer.
In English: I testify that there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His messenger. Two sentences, said in a breath or two.
Muslims place them first among the pillars of their faith: the testimony, the shahadah. And the days ahead stay with these two sentences alone.

teach.b: Start with the verb both sentences begin with. Not I think, not I feel. I testify.
I bear witness. It's a witness's word, for someone who has seen something and will say so in front of others. It turns a belief into a statement made out loud, with your name on it.
And in the Qur'an, the first to testify isn't a person at all.
Pickthall's translation of surah three: "Allah (Himself) is witness that there is no God save Him. And the angels and the men of learning (too are witness)."
So a Muslim saying the shahadah joins a line of witnesses that, in the Qur'an's picture, begins with God. Next, the first sentence, about God: there is no god but Allah.
A no, then a yes, and each half gets a day of its own.

teach.h: ONE ABOUT GOD, ONE ABOUT A PERSON.
teach.b: Then the second sentence, about a person: Muhammad is His messenger. It answers a question the first leaves open: if there is one God, how do people know how to live toward Him?
Through the messenger, who brought the message and showed it. Last, where the two sentences live.

teach.h: IN THE CALL, THE PRAYER, THE LAST BREATH.
teach.b: In the call to prayer, out loud, several times a day. Inside the prayer, said quietly while sitting. Whispered by people at the end of their lives.

And said by someone becoming Muslim, a day of its own later this week. Short enough for a child to learn, deep enough for a lifetime of asking what each word means. That's why Muslims can say two sentences hold it all.

how: Muslims hear the shahadah in every call to prayer and recite it while sitting in the ritual prayer; some say it on waking and before sleep, and it is the declaration a person makes on becoming Muslim.

o: a yearly gift to the poor, given at the end of Ramadan
the testimony: no god but Allah, Muhammad is His messenger
a daily prayer said five times between dawn and night

s: the shahadah begins with I believe
each sentence begins ashhadu, I testify: a witness's word, said out loud.
in the Qur'an, God is the first to bear witness to His oneness
"Allah (Himself) is witness that there is no God save Him."
the shahadah is said only once in a Muslim's life
it's in the call to prayer, inside the prayer, and often at the end of life.

games.q: a friend asks you for the shortest way to say what Muslims believe. what does the tradition hand you?
o: a long creed with many clauses.
a list of rules for daily life.
games.why: the shahadah: no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger. short enough for a child, deep enough for a lifetime of study.

practice: If you're Muslim, say the shahadah once at half your usual speed, stopping on each word long enough to mean it: I testify, no god, but Allah, Muhammad, His messenger.
If you're not, simply hear the words in your mind as the words Muslims say, and notice which one you'd most like to ask about. Either way, let the last word fade, and sit in the quiet after it.

wordCard.voice: Shahadah. The testimony: two sentences that bear witness to one God and His messenger. Today's word.

orig.note: testimony; each of its two sentences opens with أَشْهَدُ (ash-ha-du), I testify.

carryVoice: Your line: two sentences hold it all. A whole faith, short enough to say in one breath. Next, the first word of it: no.
